title: What is a sealed class/interface, what are the `permits` rules, and what must permitted subclasses be (`final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed`)?
shortTitle: Sealed classes/interfaces — what they are, the `permits` rules, and what permitted subclasses must be

s1_definition.profdef: A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it. You declare it with the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause listing the exact set of allowed direct subtypes. Every permitted direct subclass must itself be declared `final` (no further subclassing), `sealed` (continues the restriction with its own permits list), or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy for unrestricted subclassing). This gives the author precise, compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines the concept of an "Account" and declares by policy that only three specific account products may ever be a kind of Account: Savings, Current, and Loan — and no branch may invent a fourth type without head-office approval. Head office writes this list on an official circular. Each listed product must then state its own policy: it is either a final product that cannot be sub-divided, a further sealed product that permits only its own named variants, or an open product that any branch may extend freely. This head-office-controlled, explicitly-listed, closed family of account types is a sealed hierarchy.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed type uses `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend it, and each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it. You declare it with the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause listing the exact set of allowed direct subtypes. Every permitted direct subclass must itself be declared `final` (no further subclassing), `sealed` (continues the restriction with its own permits list), or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy for unrestricted subclassing). This gives the author precise, compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India defines the concept of an "Account" and declares by policy that only three specific account products may ever be a kind of Account: Savings, Current, and Loan — and no branch may invent a fourth type without head-office approval. Head office writes this list on an official circular. Each listed product must then state its own policy: it is either a final product that cannot be sub-divided, a further sealed product that permits only its own named variants, or an open product that any branch may extend freely. This head-office-controlled, explicitly-listed, closed family of account types is a sealed hierarchy.

**One line to remember:** A sealed type uses `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend it, and each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.

sections.s2_technical:
You declare a sealed type by adding the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause: `public sealed interface Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount { }`. This tells the compiler that the only direct subtypes of `Account` are those three named types. Any other class trying to implement `Account` is a **compile error**. This closes the hierarchy, so the author and the compiler both know the complete set of possibilities.

The **`permits` clause rules** are strict. The permitted subtypes must be **accessible** to the sealed type at compile time. In a **named module**, permitted subtypes may be in different packages of the same module. Outside modules, on the classpath, they must be in the **same package** as the sealed type. Each permitted subtype must **directly** extend or implement the sealed type; you list direct children only, not grandchildren. And every name in the `permits` list must actually exist and genuinely extend or implement the sealed type, otherwise it is a compile error.

The most important rule is what each **permitted subclass must be**. Every direct permitted subclass is required to carry exactly one of three modifiers. **`final`** means that subclass cannot itself be extended — the hierarchy ends there, which is the common choice for a concrete leaf like `SavingsAccount`. **`sealed`** means that subclass continues the sealing, so it must have its own `permits` list naming its allowed children, letting you build a multi-level closed hierarchy. **`non-sealed`** means that subclass deliberately reopens the hierarchy, so anyone may extend it without restriction — you use this when one branch of the family must remain extensible, for example a `non-sealed` base for third-party plugins. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the code does not compile.

A key detail is that you may **omit the `permits` clause** when all permitted subtypes are declared in the **same source file** as the sealed type; the compiler then infers the permitted set from the file. This is convenient for small, closed hierarchies written together. For `record` subtypes, records are implicitly `final`, so a permitted record satisfies the "must be final/sealed/non-sealed" rule automatically without you writing `final`.

The **benefits** are strong typing and exhaustiveness. Because the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, it can verify that a `switch` over a sealed type covers every case, enabling exhaustive pattern matching without a `default` branch. It also documents intent precisely: readers know no hidden subtype exists. In banking this is powerful for modelling a fixed set of account products, transaction types, or settlement states, where accidentally adding an unhandled subtype would be a serious bug.

A senior nuance is that sealing is an **author-controlled design decision** about extensibility, distinct from `final` on a single class, because it allows a known, limited set of subtypes rather than none. Another nuance is that sealed types combine with **records and pattern matching** to form algebraic data types, giving Java a safe, closed way to model "one of these shapes." A final nuance is that the sealed constraint is enforced at **compile time and recorded in the class file** via a `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, so the JVM also rejects non-permitted subtypes at load time, making the restriction robust even against bytecode tricks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must model its account products as a fixed, known set: Savings, Current, and Loan. If a developer accidentally creates a fourth, unhandled account type, downstream code that computes interest or fees could silently misbehave. We need the compiler to guarantee only these three types exist. This is exactly a sealed interface with a `permits` list.

Problem 2 — Each product needs a clear extension policy. Savings and Current are concrete leaves that must never be sub-divided, so they are `final`. Loan has sub-products (home loan, car loan) that are also a closed set, so Loan is itself `sealed` with its own permits. One special product line must remain open for future third-party add-ons, so it is `non-sealed`. This demonstrates all three required modifiers.

Problem 3 — A fee calculator switches over the account type and must handle every case. Because the hierarchy is sealed, the compiler guarantees exhaustiveness, so forgetting a case is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` interface permitting `SavingsAccount` (final), `CurrentAccount` (final), and `LoanAccount` (sealed), where `LoanAccount` permits `HomeLoan` (final) and a `non-sealed PromoAccount` branch, then a fee calculator that pattern-switches exhaustively, logging results.

The code contains: the sealed `Account`, its permitted subtypes with each modifier, a `FeeCalculator`, and a `main`.

```bash
# Verify Java version
java -version   # must be 17 or higher
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four accounts — a savings account for Rajesh, a current account for Priya, a home loan for Rajesh, and a promo account for Priya.

Step 1 — `main` builds a list of four `Account` values. Each concrete object is one of the permitted subtypes. The compiler already guaranteed, at compile time, that no other subtype of `Account` can exist.

Step 2 — For each account the code calls `calc.monthlyFee(account)`. Inside, a `switch` pattern-matches on the concrete type. Because `Account` and `LoanAccount` are sealed, the compiler knows the full set — savings, current, home loan, promo — and verifies every case is handled, so no `default` branch is needed.

Step 3 — For the savings account the fee is zero. For the current account it is a flat 200.00. For the home loan it is 0.05% of the balance, computed with `BigDecimal` and half-up rounding to two decimals, which on 3,000,000 is 1,500.00. For the promo account it is a nominal 10.00.

Step 4 — Each fee is logged with the holder and account id. The hierarchy's sealing meant that if a developer later added a new permitted subtype but forgot to add a case here, the code would fail to compile, catching the bug immediately.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) monthly fee = Rs.0
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Priya Sharma (CUR3001) monthly fee = Rs.200.00
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Rajesh Kumar (LN5001) monthly fee = Rs.1500.00
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Priya Sharma (PR7001) monthly fee = Rs.10.00
```

```
                        SavingsAccount  CurrentAccount     sealed LoanAccount

                                                                 │

                                                       ▼                   ▼
                                                   HomeLoan            PromoAccount

    SavingsAccount → 0
    CurrentAccount → 200.00
    HomeLoan       → balance × 0.0005 → 3,000,000 → 1500.00
    PromoAccount   → 10.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other types may extend or implement it. I declare it with the sealed modifier and a permits clause that names the exact set of allowed direct subtypes, and any other type trying to extend it is a compile error. This gives me, the author, precise and compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy, which is stronger than final on a single class because it allows a known, limited set of subtypes rather than none at all.

The permits rules are strict. The listed subtypes must be accessible to the sealed type, and I list only direct children, not grandchildren. In a named module the permitted subtypes may live in different packages of the same module, but on the plain classpath they must be in the same package as the sealed type. I can also omit the permits clause entirely if all the subtypes are declared in the same source file, in which case the compiler infers the set.

The most important rule is what each permitted subclass must be. Every direct permitted subclass must carry exactly one of three modifiers. Final means it cannot be extended further, which is the usual choice for a concrete leaf. Sealed means it continues the restriction and must have its own permits list, which lets me build a multi-level closed hierarchy. Non-sealed means it deliberately reopens that branch so anyone may extend it without restriction, which I use when one part of the family must stay extensible. If a permitted subclass omits all three, the code does not compile, and records satisfy the rule automatically because records are implicitly final.

In my banking project I model account products as a sealed Account interface permitting savings, current, and loan, where savings and current are final leaves, loan is itself sealed with its own permits for home loan and a non-sealed promo branch. The real payoff is exhaustiveness: because the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, my fee calculator can switch over the account type with no default branch, and the compiler guarantees every case is covered. If a teammate later adds a new permitted product but forgets to handle it, the build fails immediately rather than misbehaving in production, which is exactly the safety a bank needs for a fixed set of products.

---

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
